newsitem.title: CHINA: China sees end to small state firm reform by 2000.
newsitem.headline: China sees end to small state firm reform by 2000.

text.p: China expects to complete ambitious reforms to transform about 90 percent of its 350,000 mostly small-scale state-owned firms by the end of the century, government economists said on Wednesday.

However, the path to reform was fraught with difficulty and no sweeping initiatives could be expected that might involve political risk to China's Communist Party rulers, said the officials of the State Commission for Restructuring Economic Systems.

China had already achieved some success in its policy to reform state-owned enterprises launched last year under the slogan "focus on the big, let go of the small", said Cao Yuanzheng, deputy director of the commission's Institute on Economic System Reform.
Of China's estimated 350,000 state-owned enterprises, about 90 percent are small-scale firms, Cao said.
"In more developed areas, about 70 percent of small enterprises have completed reform while in more backward and less developed areas, the figure is about 10 percent," Cao said.
"So I estimate that within this century we can basically solve the problem of small enterprises," he said.
"If China can solve this problem of small enterprises within this century...then all other problems will be much easier to deal with."

China's leaders appear to have agreed that tackling real restructuring of the huge -- and flagging -- state sector is among the most crucial reforms remaining to be implemented under late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's vision of a "socialist market economy".
Restructuring small enterprises involved such measures as sell-offs, leasing, mergers and -- as a last resort -- bankruptcy, Cao said.

Many had chosen a route unique to China of "stock cooperation" under which stockholders were entitled to one vote per person regardless of how many stocks they held but with a dividend according to shares held, Cao said.

Such employee buyouts had proved to be an effective way to eliminate high levels of outstanding debt to banks since banks would re-allocate the credit at low rates of interest to the new owners of the enterprise, he said.
China has said it wants to get rid of most state firms, leaving the government with a core of about 1,000 companies in the strategic, defence, utilities and high-technology sectors.
However, institute deputy director Zou Dongtao cited flaws in the "focus on the big, let go of the small" strategy, and stressed that the system was an exploratory pilot scheme.
Zou has said that one problem was how to define what constituted a small state firm.
"China is not going to adopt any reforms that contain any large political risk," Zou cautioned. "It will rather move gradually."

Economists and analysts say that finding the courage to push ahead with unpalatable reforms of the flagging and long cosseted state sector will almost certainly be a hot topic at a crucial five-yearly Communist Party congress in late September.

China has moved slowly in its reform of lumbering state firms, hampered by fears that the state would lose its predominance and that bankruptcies and streamlining would result in mass unemployment and social unrest -- anathema to China's communist leadership.
